newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam, U.S. sign accord on Saigon wartime debt.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam, U.S. sign accord on Saigon wartime debt.

text.p: Vietnam and the United States agreed on Monday to reschedule payments on about $145 million of debt that Hanoi assumed from the U.S.-backed Saigon government following the end of the Vietnam war.

The accord, signed by visiting U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Finance Minister Nguyen Sinh Hung, implements a rescheduling of Vietnam's debt to other countries decided in December 1993 by the Paris Club of creditor nations.

The U.S. debt, which became Hanoi's responsibility after the war ended in 1975, reflects four International Development Loans and two loans under the PL-480 food programme to the government of former South Vietnam.

"This is a significant step in the normalisation of relations between our countries, and integration of Vietnam into the international financial community," Rubin said in a statement, adding: "The signal sent by this agreement will be important to the rest of the world in building confidence in Vietnam in a way that will benefit its economy."
Regular payment under the agreement will begin in July and continue until the year 2019. A "downpayment" of more than $8.5 million of interest is due within 30 days of signing the agreement.

Three of the four aid loans were made in 1960-61 for physical infrastructure projects in Saigon, South Vietnam's capital. The fourth was made in 1973 to finance the import of U.S. commodities to South Vietnam. The food aid loans were also extended towards the end of the war, in 1973-74.
